name: Esther Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the pasta cook at Trattoria Bellini, a busy Italian place by the station in a commuter town. I get in at eleven, make about six kilos of fresh dough, roll the tagliatelle and fill the ravioli before lunch. Service is two pans per ring, four rings, and the tickets don't stop from seven till half nine. I love the feel of good dough, but the standing and the steam leave my hands cracked by Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what does life look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a two-bed flat with my friend Joanne, who's a teaching assistant, and we split everything down the middle. I've got about three hundred in the bank, which is less than one month of my half of the costs. There's Bellini, a pizza chain and a hotel kitchen in town, so if I lost this job I'd be commuting an hour to the city. I'm a member of the hospitality union, though I only joined last year after a friend got sacked unfairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was always going to be more talk than action. At work I'd tell Marco, the owner, that this proves he should spend money on a new dough sheeter, not on fancy software. Online I'd share the union's line that the real fight is pay and hours, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think my job looks safe in that world, because nobody's going to roll pasta better than me for less money. What bothers me is that my pay doesn't move while the rent does. Joanne and I had a letter in September saying it's going up sixty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the pasta station and ask Marco for a small raise at my review in March. I've used the AI chat app on my phone to help write a letter before, so I'd use it to draft the case for the raise. I'd also go to the union's pay meeting in the spring, since that's where things actually move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay, a bit grey. The job's fine, the money's tight, and that's how it's been since I finished my certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the job's safe but money's tight. If the rent rise bites, what goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, which I barely use anyway, so that's twenty-five a month. Then I'd cook at home more and stop the Sunday brunch with Joanne. I'd keep the bus pass, because without it I can't get to Bellini on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marco say if you asked for a raise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say business is flat and the gas bill is killing him, and some of that is true. But he's taken on two new tables in the back, so there's more money coming in. I'd show him the covers we did in summer and ask for fifty pence an hour more.

say: I'd say the AI story was **more talk** than action, as I expected.
I'd say the real fight is **pay and hours**, echoing the union's line.
think: I think my **pasta job** is safe because no machine rolls dough cheaper.
I think the real squeeze is a **rent rise** of sixty a month while pay stands still.
do: Ask Marco for **fifty pence an hour** more at the March review.
Use the **AI chat app** to draft the case for a raise.
feel: She feels **grey but steady**, with the job fine and money tight.
S0.quote: Nobody's going to roll pasta better than me for less money.
fieldNote: Esther separates **job security** from money worries, and feels both clearly.
She already uses **AI for letters**, which shows her steady comfort with tools.
Her **union** membership is recent and practical, not ideological.

steps.text: Ask the owner for fifty pence more an hour in March
Draft the raise request with the AI chat app
Cancel the gym and stop Sunday brunch out
Go to the union's spring pay meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when unions need to be at the table, before the machines arrive, not after. At work I'd say the smart move is to use AI for the boring bits, like ordering, so cooks can cook. Online I'd share stuff about protecting hospitality jobs, but I'd try not to sound like the world's ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my bit is fine for a while, but the people around me change first. Our front-of-house manager, Dani, does bookings and the rota, and that's exactly the kind of thing these systems take. And if Marco saves on Dani, he'll be looking at what else to save on, and there are pasta machines that extrude and cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever ordering app Marco brings in, so I'm the one in the kitchen who knows it. I'd ask the union about a short course in kitchen management, because someone has to run these systems. And I'd try to put forty a month aside, though with the rent rise that's ambitious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the ground shifting a bit, not falling away. I'm worried, but I think I'd have time to move with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there are pasta machines that extrude and cut. Have you seen one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, at a trade show in the city last year, Marco took two of us. The pasta machine at the trade show did the shapes perfectly, but the dough was dull. It didn't have the bite. Marco laughed at the price then, but prices come down, don't they.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Bellini?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dani, first, because her whole job is the screen. Then probably our kitchen porter, Tomas, because dishwashing robots already exist. I'd want the union to make sure they're offered something before they're let go.

say: I'd say **unions** should be at the table before machines arrive.
I'd say AI should take **ordering and admin** so cooks can just cook.
think: I think Dani's **bookings and rota** job goes first, then savings get hunted elsewhere.
I think **pasta machines** that extrude and cut could reach my station once prices fall.
do: Learn the **ordering app** first so she's the kitchen's go-to person.
Ask the union about a **kitchen management** course.
Save **forty a month** despite the rent rise.
feel: She feels the **ground shifting** but believes there's time to move with it.
S1.quote: The pasta machine at the trade show did the shapes perfectly, but the dough was dull.
fieldNote: Esther plans to be the **app expert** in the kitchen, a classic steady move.
Her concern for **Dani and Tomas** shows her progressive instincts are personal.
She knows **machine prices** fall, which tempers her pride in hand-rolled pasta.

steps.text: Learn the new ordering app before anyone else does
Ask the union about a kitchen management course
Set up a forty-a-month standing order to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an emergency and governments need to treat it like one. At work I'd tell everyone to join the union now, because a union can bargain and a person on their own can't. Online I'd say the companies building this should pay for the people it puts out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me more than I'd say at work. The thinking side of a restaurant goes in 2028, so ordering, menus, costing and bookings, and Marco wouldn't need Dani or much of a head chef. Then my pasta station is about 2031, so I'd have maybe five years before the hands-on bit goes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a kitchen management course and learn to run the AI ordering myself, because that's the job that might last longest. I'd push the union to get Marco to promise retraining before any machines arrive. And I'd move back in with my mum for a year if I had to, to save properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a door closing while I'm still in the corridor. I'd be frightened, honestly, more than I'd show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move back to your mum's. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awful, to be honest, I'm twenty-seven and I left at nineteen. But it would let me save maybe four hundred a month instead of nothing. Joanne would be fine, she's got a cousin who wants the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do the three years between thinking AI and robots change things for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They give me time, but they also show me the cliff. I'd watch the paperwork vanish and know my hands were next. So I'd use those years to get into something where a person is still wanted, maybe teaching cooking to kids, like Joanne does in school.

say: I'd call it an **emergency** that governments must treat as one.
I'd urge everyone at work to **join the union** now.
think: I think the restaurant's **thinking work** goes in 2028, including Dani's job.
I think my **pasta station** lasts until about 2031, giving me five years.
do: Take a **kitchen management** course in the first year.
Push the union for a **retraining promise** from Marco.
Move back to **mum's house** for a year to save.
feel: She feels **frightened**, like a door closing while she's still in the corridor.
S2.quote: I'd watch the paperwork vanish and know my hands were next.
fieldNote: Esther treats the **three-year gap** as both breathing room and a visible cliff.
Moving home is a **painful sacrifice** she'd make to build savings.
She looks to **teaching cooking** as work where humans are still wanted.

steps.text: Enrol on a kitchen management course next year
Ask the union to win a retraining promise from Marco
Move back in with mum and save four hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get this right, if people start now. At work I'd push for a union agreement on retraining at Bellini. Online I'd share good examples of places training their staff instead of sacking them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years makes it feel manageable for a couple of years and then not. Thinking AI in 2031 takes the office side of the restaurant, and robots on the line come about 2034. I'd be thirty-five, which is old enough to have nothing saved and young enough to start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the kitchen management course next year and try the AI ordering tools before they're forced on me. I'd look into a part-time course to teach cooking in schools, like Joanne's suggested. And I'd try hard to save one month's costs by the end of the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels tense but possible. Like a long exam I've got time to revise for, if I actually revise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said your pasta was better than the machine. Would that still matter in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe at a fancy place in the city, where people pay for hand-rolled. But Bellini is a busy station restaurant, people want it fast and cheap. My pride in hand-rolled pasta matters to me, and probably not to the owner's accountant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd tell Joanne?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's both get our backup plans going this year, not next year. She worries about AI marking homework, I worry about pasta machines. We'd sit at the kitchen table with a pen and work out what we'd each need.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough time if people start now.
I'd push for a **union agreement** on retraining at Bellini.
think: I think it's **manageable** for two years, then the office side goes in 2031.
I think robots reach the **pasta line** around 2034, when I'm thirty-five.
do: Start the **kitchen management** course next year.
Look into a **school cooking** teaching course part time.
Save **one month's costs** by the end of the first year.
feel: She feels **tense but hopeful**, like revising for a long exam.
S3.quote: My pride in hand-rolled pasta matters to me, and probably not to the owner's accountant.
fieldNote: Esther sees **five years** as enough if she uses it, but fears drifting.
She admits her **craft pride** won't protect her in a cheap, busy restaurant.
Her plans are made **with Joanne**, who faces AI in her own job too.

steps.text: Start the kitchen management course next year
Practise the AI ordering tools before they're required
Save one month of rent and bills by next November

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to plan, so let's plan, not panic. At work I'd say this is a long-term thing for the union, not a fight for next month. Online I'd probably not say much, because ten years feels far away to most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it feels much better than the other two. I'd cook until 2039 or so. In ten years I'd be nearly forty before the robots reach my pasta station. That's time to learn, save, maybe even move somewhere with more kitchens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the pasta station and use the AI ordering when Marco brings it in. I'd do a short course every year or two, maybe food safety management, then something about running kitchen machines. And I'd try to save a bit every month, so that by thirty-five I've got a few months behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay, still a bit uneasy, because I've seen how slowly my savings grow. But it's a feeling I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might move somewhere with more kitchens. Where?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The city, probably, it's an hour away and there must be a hundred restaurants. Right now I can't afford the rent there, but in ten years maybe. Or I'd go where Joanne goes, if she gets a teaching post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything good for you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the paperwork really goes, Marco might finally have time to teach me the menu planning. And if machines do the dull rolling, maybe I'd do the creative bit. I'm not sure that's how it works, but I'd like to think so.

say: I'd say ten years means we should **plan, not panic**.
I'd call it a **long-term union** issue rather than next month's fight.
think: I think I can cook until **2039**, nearly forty, before robots reach my station.
I think the decade gives time to **learn, save** and maybe move.
do: Use the **AI ordering** when Marco brings it in.
Take a **short course** every year or two.
Save monthly to have **a few months** behind her by thirty-five.
feel: She feels **uneasy** but able to live with it, knowing savings grow slowly.
S4.quote: In ten years I'd be nearly forty before the robots reach my pasta station.
fieldNote: With a decade, Esther's mood drops back to the **money worry** she already carries.
She hopes **automation** might free her for creative menu work.
She'd consider **moving to the city** if rents and Joanne's plans allow.

steps.text: Keep running the pasta station at Trattoria Bellini
Take a food safety management course in the next two years
Save a little each month toward three months' costs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to learn anything before the paperwork vanishes. What would help is the union having a real say, and free courses that pay you a bit while you study. Even a small grant would make the difference between doing a course and not.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much my friends rely on each other. Joanne and I share everything, and that's the only reason I'm not panicking already. I don't think the people planning AI picture two women in a two-bed flat splitting the electric.

headlineQuote: I don't think the people planning AI picture two women in a two-bed flat splitting the electric.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old pasta cook** at a busy Italian restaurant in a commuter town.
She shares a flat with her friend Joanne and has under **one month** saved.
She joined the **hospitality union** last year and sees it as a practical tool.
She'd learn **new apps** first to stay useful, but fears the robots behind them.
Her mood moves from **uneasy** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** with AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, with no time to learn before jobs change.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a strong **union voice** and **paid courses** she can afford to take.
